passage: In a small flat in Valencia, Pablo pushes a toy car along the floor and under the sofa. Noa, one, follows it with her eyes, head turning. When it vanishes, she doesn't stare at the spot where it went in. She crawls straight to the other end of the sofa and waits, eyes on the gap. The car rolls out; she squeals and grabs it. Pablo tries again, faster. This time her eyes are already on the far side.

qa.q: Where did Noa wait for the car?
qa.a: At the other end of the sofa, watching the gap.

qa.q: What does Noa crawling to the far end suggest she expected?
qa.a: She expected the car to come out on the other side, and her squeal when it did shows she was excited and delighted to be right.

qa.q: How could Pablo make this game a little harder for Noa?
qa.a: He could use a longer tunnel or change the speed, and see whether she still waits at the right end.

qa.q: What is it like for Pablo to watch Noa's eyes move ahead of the car?
qa.a: He probably feels delighted to see her start predicting where things go. 😊

grounding: Shows a toddler following a moving toy with her eyes and predicting where it will come out.

passage: I'm Sharmila, and I was on the terrace with my baby sister Sonali when the kites were up. She kept her eyes on a green kite as it dipped and rose. When it swooped behind the water tank, she turned her head and stared at the other side of the tank, mouth open, before it came back into view. Then she bounced and pointed. I can't know what she was thinking, but it looked like she knew where it would pop out.

qa.q: Where did the green kite go out of view?
qa.a: Behind the water tank.

qa.q: What does Sonali's bouncing and pointing suggest she felt?
qa.a: She seemed excited, maybe pleased that the kite came back where she was looking.

qa.q: How could Sharmila play with Sonali using this skill?
qa.a: She could roll a ball behind a box and let Sonali watch for where it comes out.

qa.q: How might their parents react if Sharmila told them about the kite?
qa.a: They would likely be pleased to hear Sonali is following moving things and guessing where they will show up.

grounding: Shows a sibling noticing a toddler track a kite and look ahead to where it reappears.

passage: Sunday: from their window, Farhan, fourteen months, hears the train and looks around, but the carriages have passed by the time he finds them. Vinita, his mother, points. Wednesday: he catches the engine and follows it until it disappears behind the water tower, then looks at her. The next Monday, when it slides behind the tower, his eyes jump to the other side and wait. The engine appears. He squeals and slaps the windowsill.

qa.q: What does the train disappear behind?
qa.a: The water tower.

qa.q: What might Farhan have been expecting when his eyes jumped to the other side?
qa.a: He seemed eager and excited, expecting the engine to come out there, and he squealed with delight when it did.

qa.q: How did Vinita help early on, and why did it work?
qa.a: By pointing to the train, she showed him where to look, so he could start following it himself.

qa.q: What would change if Vinita never stood with him at the window?
qa.a: Farhan would have fewer daily chances to practise following the train, and she would miss seeing his progress.

grounding: Shows a toddler's eye tracking improving over days until he anticipates where the train will reappear.

passage: In the Mumbai flat, Maria, ten months, lay on the mat while her uncle Imran rolled a red ball slowly across the floor. Her eyes followed it all the way to the sofa. When it rolled underneath, she stared at the other side, waiting. The ball came out. She kicked her legs and squealed. Imran rolled it again. This time Maria looked at the other side before it even disappeared.

qa.q: What colour was the ball Imran rolled?
qa.a: The ball was red.

qa.q: What does Maria kicking and squealing suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she was excited and happy when the ball came out where she expected.

qa.q: How can Imran keep building Maria's tracking skills?
qa.a: He can keep rolling toys slowly behind objects so she can practise predicting where they'll come out.

qa.q: How might Imran feel watching Maria look ahead the second time?
qa.a: He might feel delighted and amazed that she had already learned where the ball would reappear.

grounding: Shows a baby following a moving ball with her eyes and anticipating where it will reappear.

passage:
"Arnab, watch the train!"
Manjula, Arnab's mother, pushes the toy train through a cardboard tunnel.
Arnab, eleven months, stares at the tunnel entrance.
"Where did it go?"
His eyes slide to the other end.
"Choo-choo!" The train pops out.
Arnab squeals and bangs the floor.
"Again?"
This time Arnab looks at the far end before the train even goes in.
"You knew!" Manjula laughs.

qa.q: What did Manjula push through the tunnel?
qa.a: She pushed a toy train through a cardboard tunnel.

qa.q: What does Arnab looking at the far end before the train goes in suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he expected it to come out there, and was excited to see it.

qa.q: How can Manjula keep supporting Arnab's tracking?
qa.a: She could vary the speed and path of the train so he keeps practising following and predicting.

qa.q: How does Manjula feel when Arnab looks ahead?
qa.a: She's delighted and laughs, seeing that he has learned where the train will appear.

grounding: Shows a baby tracking a moving train and anticipating where it will reappear.
